turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a good market offer, but not yet a compelling “leave a job I like” offer.** I would **negotiate—not accept immediately and not walk away yet**.

Your leverage is unusually strong:

- You’re currently well compensated.
- You weren’t looking.
- You’re happy at Meta.
- Google has already decided it wants you.
- The offer provides only a modest four-year premium unless refresh grants materialize.

I would ask for:

- **$260,000 base**
- **$1.4 million in new-hire RSUs**
- **$125,000 sign-on bonus**

A realistic negotiated outcome might be:

- **$250,000–$260,000 base**
- **$1.2 million–$1.35 million RSUs**
- **$75,000–$125,000 sign-on**

I would be reluctant to move for less than approximately **$600,000 of annualized initial compensation plus a meaningful sign-on**, unless you strongly prefer the Google role for nonfinancial reasons.

---

## How good is the current offer?

### Headline comparison

| Component | Meta currently | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $235,000 |
| Bonus | ~$36,000 | $47,000 target |
| Annualized equity | ~$250,000 | $270,000 average |
| Annualized TC | **~$526,000** | **~$552,000** |

On a simple grant-value basis, Google is offering only about **$26,000 more per year**, or **5% above your current compensation**.

Over four years, assuming flat stock prices, full target bonuses, no future Meta refreshers, and no Google refreshers:

- Google: **$2.208 million**
- Meta at your current run rate: **$2.104 million**
- Four-year advantage: only **$104,000**

That is not much compensation for switching costs, execution risk, cultural risk, loss of internal reputation, and giving up a job you already know you like.

### Market positioning

Recent compensation data places median Bay Area Google L6 PM compensation at roughly **$551,000**, while another recent US L6 dataset shows a median of approximately **$514,000**, median base of $240,000, and 90th-percentile TC around $671,000. In other words, your offer is broadly **around market median**, not a premium or top-of-band package. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Your $235,000 base is:

- $5,000 below your Meta base.
- Close to the reported $240,000 L6 PM median.
- Above the midpoint of the posted $183,000–$271,000 range, but still $36,000 below its maximum.

The equity is the strongest component. The absence of any sign-on is the clearest weakness.

---

## The vesting schedule is critical

Before deciding, get the **exact GSU vesting schedule in writing**.

Current reporting indicates Google new-hire grants commonly vest **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, while refresh grants generally vest evenly. However, your individual award agreement controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

If your $1.08 million grant follows 38/32/20/10 and the stock price remains unchanged:

| Year | Equity vesting | Approx. Google TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |

That makes the offer much more attractive in years one and two, but it creates a significant year-three/year-four decline.

Your next 12 months at Meta are approximately:

- $240,000 base
- $36,000 bonus
- $200,000 known vesting
- **$476,000 total**

So Google could beat your upcoming Meta year by approximately **$216,000** if the 38% first-year schedule applies. But that is mostly timing: the four-year economics remain only modestly better before refreshers.

If the grant instead vests 25% each year, Google would be approximately **$552,000 every year** before stock movement and refreshes.

---

## Do not value refresh grants as guaranteed compensation

Google confirms that equity refresh amounts are part of its annual compensation process and depend on factors including performance, location, role, modeled recommendations, and management discretion. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

Therefore:

- Treat refreshers as **upside**, not as part of the offer.
- Do not let the recruiter close a guaranteed-compensation gap with “refresh grants will stack.”
- Ask for historical or illustrative numbers, but don’t include them in your minimum acceptable package.

The recruiter was appropriately transparent that they are not guaranteed.

---

## What exactly to ask for

### Recommended opening request

Ask for all three components:

1. **Base: $260,000**
   - Within the posted range.
   - Reflects that you already make $240,000.
   - Gives room to settle around $250,000–$255,000.

2. **New-hire RSUs: $1.4 million**
   - Your $1.08 million is solid but produces only $552,000 average annual TC.
   - $1.4 million, combined with $260,000 base and a 20% bonus, produces about **$662,000 annualized TC**.
   - That is around the upper end—but still close to the reported L6 90th-percentile TC of approximately $671,000. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/))

3. **Sign-on: $125,000**
   - Position it as compensation for leaving a strong situation and forfeiting near-term Meta equity.
   - I would ask for $125,000–$150,000 if you’re comfortable anchoring aggressively.
   - Be prepared for Google to trade between sign-on and RSUs.

### Your likely acceptable landing zone

A particularly clean target would be:

- $250,000 base
- $1.2 million RSUs
- $75,000–$100,000 sign-on

That produces:

- $250,000 base
- $50,000 target bonus
- $300,000 average grant value
- **$600,000 annualized TC**
- Plus the sign-on

A stronger landing point would be $250,000–$260,000 base, $1.3 million RSUs, and $100,000 sign-on.

### Priority order

If they won’t move on everything, prioritize:

1. **RSUs**
2. **Sign-on**
3. **Base**

Equity has the greatest ability to change the package. Sign-on compensates for the immediate transition. Base is recurring and affects bonus, but a $10,000 base increase only adds another $2,000 of target bonus.

---

## Suggested message to the recruiter

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and role. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking and I’m in a strong position at Meta, so the decision needs to make sense financially as well as professionally.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526,000, including $240,000 base, and I also have approximately $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months. On an annualized basis, the current Google package is about $552,000, so it represents only a modest premium over staying despite the risk and disruption of making a move.
>
> I’d be ready to move forward if we could bring the package closer to a $260,000 base, $1.4 million equity grant, and a $125,000 sign-on bonus. I understand there may be constraints among the components, so I’m open to different combinations, with equity and make-whole compensation being the most important.
>
> Could you take that back to the compensation team and see what flexibility exists?

Then stop talking. Don’t immediately soften the request or give them your minimum.

If they ask, “What would get you to sign today?”, you can say:

> If the team can get close to those numbers, I’m confident we can reach an agreement. I’d like to see the strongest package the compensation team can approve before committing to a precise walk-away number.

---

## Questions to resolve before accepting

Ask the recruiter to confirm in writing:

1. **The exact new-hire GSU vesting percentages and first vest date.**
2. **The date and stock price used to convert the dollar grant into shares.**
3. **Whether you’ll be eligible for the next refresh cycle.**
4. **Whether the first refresh is prorated based on start date.**
5. **How refresh grants vest.**
6. **Whether your first annual bonus will be prorated.**
7. **Whether a sign-on would have a repayment obligation and for how long.**
8. **Whether your work location is officially San Francisco and whether moving between SF and another Bay Area office affects compensation.**

It is also reasonable to ask:

> Without representing it as guaranteed, can you share the typical or target refresh range for an L6 PM receiving a “meets expectations” rating?

They may decline, but the response itself is informative.

---

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### My recommendation: **negotiate**

- **Do not walk now:** the offer is respectable and could become compelling.
- **Do not accept as-is solely for compensation:** it is essentially a median L6 offer and only a 5% annualized premium over your current package.
- **Accept as-is only if:** you materially prefer the product, manager, scope, promotion trajectory, or Google environment—and the vesting schedule is indeed front-loaded.
- **Walk if:** they refuse meaningful movement and you are genuinely happy at Meta. Staying for roughly similar four-year compensation is a completely rational decision.

Because Google approached you and you were not seeking to leave, your standard should not be “Is this fair?” It should be:

> **“Is this sufficiently better to justify leaving a situation I already like?”**

At $552,000 annualized with no sign-on, my answer is **not quite**. At roughly $600,000–$625,000 annualized plus $75,000–$125,000 sign-on, the financial case becomes substantially stronger.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs stay at $1,080,000, plus a $200,000 sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation: **take it**, assuming you’re at least reasonably positive about the role, manager, and team.

The revised package has crossed from “not enough to justify leaving” to **financially compelling**. Google effectively accepted your make-whole argument:

- Base now matches Meta: **$240,000**
- Target bonus: **$48,000**
- Annualized initial equity: **$270,000**
- Recurring annualized compensation: **$558,000**
- Sign-on: **$200,000**

Your recurring Google package is only about **$32,000—or 6%—above** your stated Meta run rate. But the $200,000 sign-on meaningfully changes the switching economics.

## Four-year comparison

Assuming target bonuses, flat stock prices, no refresh grants at either company, and your current Meta compensation continuing at approximately $526,000:

|  | Google | Meta |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base + bonus over four years | $1,152,000 | $1,104,000 |
| Initial/vesting equity | $1,080,000 | $1,000,000 |
| Sign-on | $200,000 | — |
| **Four-year total** | **$2,432,000** | **$2,104,000** |

That is a **$328,000 four-year advantage** for Google—about **$82,000 per year on average**.

The assumptions matter: neither company’s future refresh grants are guaranteed, stock prices will move, and your Meta vesting schedule may not actually remain at $250,000 annually. But based on the information you gave, this is now a legitimate premium rather than a lateral move.

Current self-reported market data puts median US Google L6 PM compensation around $514,000, with median base around $240,000. Your $558,000 recurring package is therefore above that median before counting the sign-on, although such market data mixes existing employees and offers. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

## If Google uses the common front-loaded schedule

Recent reporting indicates Google new-hire grants commonly vest 38%/32%/20%/10%, but **your actual grant agreement controls**. Alphabet publicly states only that RSUs generally vest over four years, contingent on continued employment. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If your schedule is 38%/32%/20%/10%, your compensation would look approximately like this:

| Year | Equity | Base + target bonus | Sign-on | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | $288,000 | $200,000 | **$898,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | $288,000 | — | **$633,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | $288,000 | — | **$504,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | $288,000 | — | **$396,000** |

That gives you excellent economics for the first two years but creates a meaningful year-three/year-four decline unless refresh grants fill it in.

If it is instead straight-line 25% annual vesting, your compensation would be:

- Year 1: **$758,000**
- Years 2–4: **$558,000 per year**

Either way, the first-year package substantially exceeds both your $526,000 historical run rate and the approximately $476,000 you expect at Meta over the next 12 months.

## The sign-on genuinely makes you whole—but check the clawback

The $200,000 sign-on is a reasonable gross replacement for the $200,000 of Meta RSUs you’re forfeiting. Both are generally treated as employment compensation: bonuses are taxable wages, while RSUs generally become taxable when shares are transferred at vesting. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15?utm_source=openai))

Before signing, verify:

1. **When the $200,000 is paid**
2. **Whether the clawback lasts one or two years**
3. **Whether repayment is prorated or all-or-nothing**
4. **Whether repayment is based on the gross amount**
5. **Whether involuntary termination triggers repayment**
6. **The precise equity vesting schedule and first vest date**
7. **Whether your first bonus is prorated**
8. **Whether you’re eligible for the next refresh cycle**

A two-year, all-or-nothing gross clawback is materially worse than a one-year or monthly prorated clawback. I would not necessarily reject the offer over it, but I would treat the sign-on as restricted money until the clawback expires.

Also, don’t confuse withholding with final tax liability. Supplemental wages may initially have federal income tax withheld at 22% under certain circumstances, but your actual tax is determined on your tax return and could be substantially higher at your income. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15?utm_source=openai))

## When I would still stay at Meta

I would turn Google down if one or more of these is true:

- You materially prefer your Meta manager, team, or product.
- The Google role has weaker scope or worse promotion prospects.
- You have unusually strong evidence of a large Meta refresh or near-term promotion.
- You believe you may leave Google during the sign-on clawback period.
- The $200,000 sign-on has unusually punitive repayment terms.
- You value your established internal reputation and operating effectiveness at Meta more than the approximately $328,000 modeled premium.

Compensation is now good enough. The remaining question is no longer “Is Google paying enough?” It is **“Would I be reasonably happy doing this job?”**

## My decision rule

- **Google role/team is at least as attractive as Meta:** Accept.
- **Google is slightly less attractive, but still a good opportunity:** Probably accept; the premium compensates for some risk.
- **You strongly prefer staying at Meta:** Decline. An extra modeled $328,000 over four years is not enough to spend years in a job you expect to like substantially less.
- **You’re relying on refresh grants to make the numbers work:** Don’t. The package already needs to stand on its guaranteed components.

Because you said compensation matters a lot, my lean is clear: **accept the final offer, provided the role itself is acceptable and the sign-on clawback is reasonable.** I would not reopen negotiations after they explicitly said this is their best offer; I would only clarify the written terms before signing.
